title: Within- and Between-Cycle Variability in Strength and Endurance Performance Across Multiple Menstrual Cycles in Eumenorrheic Women
summary:
Women remain underrepresented in sports science and sports medicine research. At the same time, it is still not fully understood to what extent cyclic variation in endogenous sex hormones affect exercise performance. Previous studies have produced inconsistent findings in this regard: while some studies have reported differences in objectively measured strength and endurance performance between different menstrual cycle phases, others have found no corresponding changes. In contrast, changes in perceived exercise performance have been reported more consistently.
In addition, most previous studies have investigated only a single menstrual cycle, making it unclear whether potential changes are reproducible across several consecutive cycles. Menstrual cycle-related symptoms (for example headaches, menstrual cramps) may also contribute to individual fluctuations in objectively measured and perceived exercise performance, although their relevance in this context remains insufficiently understood.

Therefore, the present study aims to investigate the variability in objectively measured exercise performance as well as perceived exercise performance within one menstrual cycle and across multiple menstrual cycles in naturally menstruating women. In addition, the study aims to examine the extent to which this variability is associated with the occurrence and severity of menstrual cycle-related symptoms.

For this purpose, trained women with natural menstrual cycles will be assessed during three different menstrual cycle phases across three consecutive menstrual cycles. At the beginning of the study, an initial visit will be conducted to verify the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Subsequently, participants will enter a lead-in cycle. During the early follicular phase of this lead-in cycle, a baseline assessment will be performed. This assessment will include the determination of the back squat one-repetition maximum as well as a ramp test on the treadmill to determine the maximal achieved running speed. The values obtained will be used to individualize the exercise intensities for the subsequent experimental sessions. A total of three experimental sessions will be conducted per menstrual cycle. These will take place during different menstrual cycle phases: the early follicular phase, late follicular phase, and mid-luteal phase. At each experimental session, resting metabolic rate will be measured, blood samples will be collected, body composition will be assessed, a back squat load-velocity profile will be performed, and a combined running step and ramp test will be conducted. In addition, ratings of perceived exertion and self-assessed exercise performance will be recorded. The occurrence and severity of menstrual cycle-related symptoms, as well as the weekly training volume, will be assessed using online questionnaires. Menstrual cycle tracking and urinary ovulation tests will be used to determine menstrual cycle phases and to schedule the experimental sessions, while 17β-estradiol and progesterone concentrations will be assessed a posteriori to verify the respective menstrual cycle phase.
conditions: Within- and between-menstrual cycle variability in strength and endurance performance in naturally menstruating (eumenorrheic) women.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
non-smoker, endurance- and strength-trained: back squat one-repetition maximum ≥ 100% body mass, VO2peak ≥ 37 ml∙min-1∙kg-1, eumenorrheic menstrual cycle
Exclusion criteria:
chronic or acute injuries that may affect exercise performance, menstrual cycle-related dysfunctions or any other conditions known to affect the hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis
